questions.knowledge_point: Calculating an Improper Integral Using a Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u={x}^{3}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u={x}^{2}\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to -\infty $ when $x\to -\infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u={x}^{3}$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $-\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $-\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{x}^{2}\cdot {5}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{5}^{u}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{x}^{2}\cdot {5}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}{5}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{{5}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }[{5}^{u}]_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(1-{5}^{a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡5}(1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{5}^{a})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y={5}^{a},$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{a\to -\infty }{5}^{a}=0$

- ${lim}_{a\to \infty }{5}^{a}=\infty $

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070214/assets/c0c7699b036ebd8779cd6c3d3143cdcca6312834ee731e144e38488124164f43.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{x}^{2}\cdot {5}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡5}(1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{5}^{a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡5}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Improper Integral Involving Other Exponential Functions
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int {b}^{\,px+q}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{p\operatorname{ln}⁡(b)}{b}^{\,px+q}+C
$$

We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{3}^{2x+2}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}{3}^{2x+2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{9\cdot {3}^{2x}}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{9}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[{3}^{2x}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{9}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }(1-{3}^{2a}) \\  & =\frac{9}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}\cdot (1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{3}^{2a})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y={3}^{2x}$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }{3}^{2x}=0$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{3}^{2x}=\infty $

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070214/assets/052e461c4f02a644254b4b9936b688c29afacd07432db7234bd71474dc9a076c.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{3}^{2x+2}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{9}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}\cdot (1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{3}^{2a}) \\  & =\frac{9}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}\cdot (1-0) \\  & =\frac{9}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating an Improper Integral Using a Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\frac{1}{x}\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to \infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $1$ | $\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{{3}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}{x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{3}^{-u}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{{3}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}{x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{3}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{3}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{{3}^{-u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{3}^{-u}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{3}^{a}}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\frac{1}{{3}^{x}},$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{3}^{x}}=\infty $

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{{3}^{x}}=0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070214/assets/fac2eaeb6dfdda240d2bad7107f7a7e26ff688e89976437a95b99bc3f2ac288f.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{{3}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}{x}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{3}^{a}}-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\cdot (0-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating an Improper Integral Using a Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=\frac{1}{x}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to -\infty $ when $x\to {0}^{-}$ and $u\to 0$ when $x\to -\infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=\frac{1}{x}$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $-\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-\infty $ | $0$ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{3/x}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{0}^{-\infty }{e}^{3u}\,\text{d}u={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{e}^{3u}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{3/x}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}{e}^{3u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{{e}^{3u}}{3}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(1-{e}^{3a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{3a})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y={e}^{3x}$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }{e}^{3x}=0$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{e}^{3x}=\infty $

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070214/assets/34abda46dc9fc2c6f14ce4f8460ba076a16004bb9141eb8074cdc08e0c12fd2f.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{3/x}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}(1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{3a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Improper Integral Involving Other Exponential Functions
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int {b}^{\,px+q}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{p\operatorname{ln}⁡(b)}{b}^{\,px+q}+C
$$

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{2}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}{2}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{{2}^{-3x}}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{2}^{-3x}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{2}^{3a}}-\frac{1}{{2}^{3}})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\frac{1}{{2}^{3x}},$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{2}^{3x}}=\infty $

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{{2}^{3x}}=0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070214/assets/998ec723fd7212da4382718750465ce313349ed3f2c0258cc1f68e0a5485d968.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{2}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{2}^{3a}}-\frac{1}{{2}^{3}}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot (0-\frac{1}{8}) \\  & =\frac{1}{24\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}.\end{aligned}
$$
